client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus at work at all — I'll be in the middle of a task and just completely lose track of what I was doing, and my boss has already noticed. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because nothing is going to bring her back.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying an enormous weight right now — the grief of losing your grandmother, the pressure at work, and maybe even a quiet exhaustion underneath it all, like part of you has gone very still. I hear some doubt about whether talking can help, and that's a completely understandable place to be when you're hurting this deeply. I'm wondering, even as you say the words, what does it feel like in your body right now to be here and talking about her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, there's this kind of heaviness in my chest, like something is just sitting there and won't move. And my throat gets tight when I start to think about her, like I'm bracing myself against something. I guess I didn't expect it to feel so physical — I thought I was just distracted and stressed, but saying it out loud makes it feel more real, and I'm not sure I like that.
therapist: What you just described — that heaviness, the tightening throat — that *is* the grief, not just a side effect of it, and your body has been holding all of this even when your mind was trying to stay focused on work. It's really significant that saying it out loud made it feel more real, because that tells me a part of you is ready to actually meet this, even if another part feels unsure. I'm curious — when you say you're not sure you like it feeling more real, what are you most afraid that "more real" might mean?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think I'm afraid that if I really let myself feel it, I won't be able to function at all — like I'll just fall apart completely and not be able to pull myself back together. I already can't focus at work, and I keep thinking if I open this up more, it's only going to get worse. It's easier to stay a little numb, even though I know that's not really working either.
therapist: That fear of falling apart completely is so common in grief, and it makes so much sense that numbness feels safer right now — it's actually been protecting you. But I want to gently offer this: what you're describing, the difficulty focusing, the heaviness, the tightness in your throat — that's the grief already coming through, even with the numbness in place. I'm wondering, has there ever been a time in your life when you let yourself feel something really difficult and actually did find your way back through it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean, maybe — when my parents divorced when I was a teenager, that was really hard, and I did eventually get through it. But that feels different somehow, because back then I was just angry, and anger kind of gives you energy to keep going. This is more like... emptiness, and I don't know how to move through something when it feels like there's nothing to push against.
therapist: You just made a really important connection — you *have* moved through something hard before, and that resilience is still part of you. But I notice that even as you're sharing this, your words are coming quickly, like there's a lot rushing forward, while something in your voice sounds quieter and more exhausted underneath — almost like you're running on fumes while trying to think your way through this. I'm wondering if part of you is working very hard right now to stay one step ahead of that emptiness, rather than letting yourself just rest in this moment with it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I think that's probably true — I've been filling every quiet moment with something, work tasks, TV, scrolling my phone, anything to avoid just sitting with it. But I'm not sure I know how to just "rest in the emptiness" like you're suggesting, because every time things get quiet, my mind just goes straight to guilt about things I didn't say to her before she died. It doesn't feel like rest, it feels like an ambush.
therapist: That word "ambush" is so vivid, and it tells me the guilt has real power over you in those quiet moments — it's not just sadness, it's something that feels like it comes for you. What you didn't say to her before she died — I want to make sure we don't rush past that, because it sounds like it might be sitting at the very center of all of this. Would you be willing to share a little about what those unspoken things are, at whatever pace feels okay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: The main thing is that I hadn't visited her in almost eight months before she died — I kept telling myself I'd go soon, that there was time, and then there wasn't. I talked to her on the phone a few times but I always kept the calls short because I was busy, and now I can't stop thinking that she probably knew I was rushing her off the line. I guess I'm telling you this, but I also feel like saying it out loud just confirms what I already believe about myself — that I was a bad grandchild, and I'm not sure therapy can really talk me out of that.
therapist: The way you just shared that — quickly, softly, like you needed to get it out before you could stop yourself — tells me how much courage it took to say it out loud. I want to reflect something back to you: you're not describing a bad grandchild, you're describing a human being who got caught in the very ordinary trap of believing there would be more time, which is something grief has a way of turning into a weapon against us. I'm not here to talk you out of anything, but I am curious — if a close friend told you they had done exactly what you just described, would you look at them and think "bad person," or would you see something more complicated than that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I know what you're doing, and I know logically I would never judge a friend that harshly — I'd probably tell them that life gets busy and their grandmother knew they loved them. But it feels completely different when it's me, like the same logic just doesn't apply, and I don't really understand why I can extend that compassion to everyone else but not to myself. It's frustrating because part of me can see the double standard, but knowing it's there doesn't make it go away.
therapist: What you just named is actually one of the most important insights in this kind of work — that seeing the double standard and *feeling* your way out of it are two completely different things, and the gap between them can be incredibly frustrating. Your voice carries something that sounds almost urgent right now, like this realization is pressing on you, which makes me think part of you genuinely wants to find a way across that gap. I'm wondering — when you imagine extending that same compassion to yourself, even just a little, what's the first thing that gets in the way?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think the first thing that gets in the way is this feeling that if I let myself off the hook, it means what I did — or didn't do — didn't matter, like compassion and accountability can't exist at the same time. It feels like forgiving myself would somehow minimize her, or minimize the fact that I should have shown up more. I know that probably sounds strange, but the guilt almost feels like the last thing I have left to give her.
therapist: That doesn't sound strange at all — it sounds like one of the most tender things I've heard, that you're holding onto the guilt because it feels like a form of love, a way of still being in relationship with her. But I want to sit with something you said: what if accountability and compassion aren't opposites, but what if the truest way to honor her is not to punish yourself, but to carry forward what you wished you'd done differently? I'm wondering — what do you think *she* would have wanted for you, if she could see you sitting here right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: She would have wanted me to be okay — I know that without even having to think about it, because she was always the person who worried about everyone else more than herself. But knowing that and actually believing I deserve to be okay feel like two completely different things, and I'm sitting here with this strange mix of feeling closer to her for a second and then immediately feeling like I don't deserve even that. I guess I'm just not sure how you actually make the leap from knowing something to feeling it.
therapist: That moment of feeling close to her — even briefly — is actually really significant, and I don't want it to get lost under the "I don't deserve it" that followed so quickly. What you're describing, that gap between knowing and feeling, is exactly the work we can do together, and it happens not through one big leap but through small moments like the one you just had, where the truth gets through for just a second. I'm wondering if we could slow down and stay with that feeling of closeness to her for just a moment longer — what was present for you in that brief instant before the doubt came in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: For just that second, I think I felt something warm, like she was actually here and not just a memory I was trying to hold onto. It was like I could almost hear her voice, the way she used to say my name, and it didn't hurt in that exact moment — it just felt like her. But it went so fast, and I'm honestly not sure I can just call that feeling back on purpose, like I'm worried that trying to hold onto it will make it disappear even faster.
therapist: What you just described — that warmth, hearing her say your name, feeling her presence rather than just the ache of her absence — that is real, and it belongs to you. I notice you're speaking quickly, like you're trying to capture something before it slips away, which makes sense because that moment felt precious and fragile. What if we didn't think of it as something to hold onto, but rather as proof that she's still accessible to you — that she hasn't gone as completely as the grief sometimes makes it feel?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
